The website cannot run Python, so the helper below will precompute the chart for every country and join the results with a menu.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with a dropdown menu.

    Like slider_figure, but each choice also sets its own axis ranges.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            compact(trace)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range,
                  "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        buttons.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down", x=1, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom")], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig
def taylor_world_chart(country="United States", r_bar=2.0):
    """Fig. 4 for other central banks: the policy rate and the Taylor rule, annual averages."""
    data = taylor_world[taylor_world.country == country]
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"year": data.year, "Policy rate": data.policy_rate,
                          "Taylor rule": taylor_rule(data.inflation, data.output_gap, r_bar)})
    late = chart[chart.year == 2022].dropna()
    gap = "no data for 2022"
    if not late.empty:
        diff = round(late["Taylor rule"].iloc[0] - late["Policy rate"].iloc[0], 1) + 0.0      # + 0.0 avoids -0.0
        gap = f"rule minus actual in 2022 = {diff:+.1f} points"
    fig = px.line(chart, x="year", y=["Policy rate", "Taylor rule"], markers=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}, r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}: {gap}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    low = min(chart["Policy rate"].min(), chart["Taylor rule"].min())
    high = max(chart["Policy rate"].max(), chart["Taylor rule"].max())
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1998.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=fit_axis(low, high, [(-5, 11.5), (-10, 20), (-15, 30)]),
                      legend_title_text="", legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig
interact(taylor_world_chart, country=Dropdown(options=sorted(taylor_world.country.unique()), value="United States",
                                              description="central bank of", style=WIDE),
         r_bar=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="r̄ in the rule (%)", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: the Taylor rule for 14 central banks (r̄ = 2), with a country menu
dropdown_figure(taylor_world_chart, "country", sorted(taylor_world.country.unique()), start="United States")

Sources. Data: Bank for International Settlements, Central bank policy rates (WS_CBPOL); OECD, Economic Outlook No. 119 (dataflow DSD_EO@DF_EO), via the OECD Data Explorer: core inflation (PCORE_YTYPCT), headline inflation (CPI_YTYPCT, else CPIH_YTYPCT) and the output gap (GAP); European Central Bank, euro-area HICP excluding energy and food (ICP.M.U2.N.XEF000.4.ANR). The Taylor rule is our own calculation. Prepared file: data/ch14/taylor_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, pick a central bank in the menu above the chart.

What to notice.

  • In 2022 every one of these central banks was far below its rule: by 6.8 points in the United States, 6.5 in the euro area and 13.8 in the United Kingdom. Inflation surprised them all at the same time. Japan, with inflation still near zero, was only 1.3 points below.
  • From 2002 to 2006 the rule was above the actual rate in the euro area too (by 1.4 points a year on average, 1.6 in the United States with annual data): “too low for too long” was not only an American story.
  • Look at your data. The OECD has no core inflation for the United Kingdom, so its rule uses headline inflation (the cell above counts those years). Pick Japan: the line has holes. From 1999 to 2006 and from 2013 to 2016 the Bank of Japan targeted the quantity of money instead of an interest rate, so the BIS records no policy rate for most of those years.

Fig. 5: What happened to potential GDP?

Goal. See how much of the “recovery” after 2008 came from a lower estimate of potential GDP.

Short-run output is the gap between actual and potential GDP. Potential GDP cannot be observed: the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates it with an extended Solow model, and it revises the estimate as new data arrive. Here we compare actual GDP with two CBO estimates of potential: the latest one, and the one the CBO made in 2007, just before the crisis.

gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-5.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
gdp.tail(3)
date gdp_actual gdp_potential_latest gdp_potential_2007
103 2025-10-01 24.1255 23.8112 NaN
104 2026-01-01 24.2744 23.9451 NaN
105 2026-04-01 24.4080 24.0709 NaN

The values are in trillions of chained 2017 dollars (the textbook used 2012 dollars, so its numbers are lower). The 2007 estimate ends in 2017, the last year the CBO projected at the time; after that the column is empty (NaN, “not a number”).

         "gdp_potential_2007": "Potential GDP, 2007 estimate"}
fig = px.line(gdp.rename(columns=names), x="date", y=list(names.values()), color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN],
              labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Trillions of 2017 dollars", "variable": "Series"},
              title="The output gap closed mostly because potential GDP was revised down")
fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[12.5, 25.5], tickvals=[14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24]), hovermode="x unified",
                  legend_title_text="", legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPC1), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED; the CBO’s 2007 estimate is the June 2007 vintage of GDPPOT in ALFRED, the archival FRED database, rebased to chained 2017 dollars. Prepared file: data/ch14/fig14-5.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Until 2002 the two estimates of potential are within half a percent of each other. Then they drift apart: the latest estimate is already 2.3 percent lower in 2007. After 2008 the 2007 estimate keeps rising along its old trend, while the latest estimate bends down.
  • Measured against the latest estimate, actual GDP was back at potential by about 2018. Measured against the 2007 estimate, it never came close.
  • Since 2018 actual GDP has been slightly above the latest estimate of potential, apart from the Covid-19 dip of 2020.

Beyond the United States: GDP, potential GDP and the old trend in OECD countries

The CBO’s estimates exist only for the United States, and old vintages of other countries’ potential GDP are hard to find. The OECD’s Economic Outlook publishes real GDP and potential GDP for its members, so we can draw the latest estimates; and we can build the “2007 view” ourselves, by extending each country’s average growth of 1997–2007 into the future. That old trend is what a forecaster who expected the pre-crisis growth to continue would have drawn. Both GDP and potential are set to 100 for actual GDP in 2007.

potential_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "potential_world.csv")
potential_world[potential_world.country == "Spain"].tail(3)
iso3 country year gdp potential_gdp
1188 ESP Spain 2023 111.682 113.602
1189 ESP Spain 2024 115.540 116.132
1190 ESP Spain 2025 118.804 118.649

Python note. np.exp undoes np.log: if GDP grows at the log rate g per year, after t years it is np.exp(g * t) times larger. rows.year - end counts the years since 2007 (negative before it), and .where(rows.year >= end) keeps the values from 2007 on and leaves the earlier cells empty. In the title, 'below' if gap < 0 else 'above' picks one of two words.

TREND = "Trend of 1997–2007, extended"


def old_trend(rows, start=1997, end=2007):
    """GDP if it had kept growing at its average 1997-2007 rate after 2007 (a log-linear trend)."""
    x = rows.set_index("year").gdp
    g = np.log(x[end] / x[start]) / (end - start)
    return (x[end] * np.exp(g * (rows.year - end))).where(rows.year >= end)
def potential_world_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 5 for OECD countries: actual GDP, the OECD's potential GDP and the 1997-2007 trend (2007 GDP = 100)."""
    rows = potential_world[(potential_world.country == country) & (potential_world.year >= 1995)]
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"year": rows.year, "Actual GDP": rows.gdp, "Potential GDP (OECD, latest)": rows.potential_gdp})
    title = f"{country}: no GDP data for 1997, so no trend"
    if 1997 in rows.year.values:
        chart[TREND] = old_trend(rows)
        y2019 = chart[chart.year == 2019].iloc[0]
        gap = 100 * (y2019["Actual GDP"] / y2019[TREND] - 1)
        title = f"{country}: in 2019 GDP was {abs(gap):.1f}% {'below' if gap < 0 else 'above'} its 1997–2007 trend"
    lines = list(chart.columns[1:])
    fig = px.line(chart, x="year", y=lines, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN], title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Index, actual GDP in 2007 = 100", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", selector=dict(name=TREND))
    y_range = fit_axis(chart[lines].min().min(), chart[lines].max().max(), [(60, 140), (40, 200), (20, 300), (20, 450)])
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1994.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=y_range, legend_title_text="",
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig
interact(potential_world_chart, country=Dropdown(options=sorted(potential_world.country.unique()), value="United States",
                                                 description="country", style=WIDE));

Sources. Data: OECD, Economic Outlook No. 119 (dataflow DSD_EO@DF_EO), via the OECD Data Explorer: real GDP (GDPV) and potential output (GDPVTR). The old trend (1997–2007 growth extended) is our own calculation. Prepared file: data/ch14/potential_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, pick a country in the menu above the chart.

What to notice.

  • The United States did not lose more than others. Its GDP in 2019 was 14.2 percent below the 1997–2007 trend; the euro area’s was 16.9 percent below, Spain’s 30.9 and Greece’s 52.4 percent. Greece’s GDP in 2025 was still 14 percent below its 2007 level.
  • Pick Germany, Japan or Israel: 5.1, 5.8 and 1.3 percent below trend. Their pre-crisis growth was slow or steady, so the old trend was easier to keep up with.
  • The OECD, like the CBO, has revised potential down to where GDP went: for the United States its potential grew 1.9 percent a year from 2007 to 2019 (the CBO: 1.8), and both estimates sit almost on top of actual GDP since 2018.
  • Look at your data. The old trend is a counterfactual, not a fact. For fast-growing economies such as Latvia, Estonia or Ireland, ten boom years extrapolated give absurd paths, and the axis widens. Ireland’s GDP also jumped 25 percent in 2015, when multinational firms moved assets there: an accounting change, not a boom in production.

Key numbers: two estimates of the output gap

def output_gap(actual, potential):
    """Short-run output: the percent gap between actual and potential GDP."""
    return 100 * (actual / potential - 1)


gdp["gap_latest"] = output_gap(gdp.gdp_actual, gdp.gdp_potential_latest)
gdp["gap_2007"] = output_gap(gdp.gdp_actual, gdp.gdp_potential_2007)
gaps = gdp.groupby(gdp.date.dt.year)[["gap_latest", "gap_2007"]].mean()
gaps.loc[[2007, 2009, 2010, 2015, 2017]].round(2)
gap_latest gap_2007
date
2007 1.19 -1.12
2009 -4.66 -8.81
2010 -3.34 -8.87
2015 -0.82 -10.22
2017 -0.63 -10.78

In 2017, actual GDP was 10.8 percent below the CBO’s 2007 estimate of potential but only 0.6 percent below the latest one. The gap closed because potential was revised down by about 10 percent, not because GDP grew fast.

Fig. 6: The growth rate of various money supply measures

Goal. Check whether the Fed repeated the mistake of the Great Depression, when the money supply collapsed.

Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Great Depression on a Fed that let the money supply fall from 1929 to 1933. Here we look at three measures of money after 1990, from the narrowest to the broadest: currency, M1 (currency plus checking accounts) and M2 (M1 plus savings accounts and small time deposits). Each is measured by its growth over the last 12 months.

money = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-6.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
money.describe().round(1)
date currency m1 m2
count 440 440.0 440.0 440.0
mean 2008-04-16 04:54:32.727272704 6.8 14.2 5.7
min 1990-01-01 00:00:00 0.6 -10.8 -4.6
25% 1999-02-22 00:00:00 4.6 1.2 3.9
50% 2008-04-16 00:00:00 7.0 5.0 5.6
75% 2017-06-08 12:00:00 8.8 9.6 6.9
max 2026-08-01 00:00:00 16.4 356.9 26.8
std NaN 3.1 54.2 4.2

A data-hygiene moment. M1 grew by 357 percent in a year? That is not money creation. In May 2020 the Fed redefined M1 to include savings deposits, so M1 jumped by about 11 trillion dollars in one month. Any 12-month growth rate that compares the new definition with the old one, from May 2020 to April 2021, is meaningless. We blank those months out instead of letting them dominate the chart.

Python note. money.loc[rows, "m1"] = np.nan replaces the values of column m1 in the selected rows with NaN, “not a number”. Plotly leaves a gap where a value is missing.

broken = (money.date >= "2020-05-01") & (money.date <= "2021-04-01")
print(f"M1 growth from May 2020 to April 2021: {money.m1[broken].min():.0f}% to {money.m1[broken].max():.0f}%")
money.loc[broken, "m1"] = np.nan                   # growth across the definition break is not money growth
print(f"M1 growth in April 2020 and May 2021: {money.m1[money.date == '2020-04-01'].iloc[0]:.1f}% and "
      f"{money.m1[money.date == '2021-05-01'].iloc[0]:.1f}%")
M1 growth from May 2020 to April 2021: 291% to 357%
M1 growth in April 2020 and May 2021: 26.9% and 18.2%
names = {"currency": "Currency", "m1": "M1", "m2": "M2"}
fig = px.line(money.rename(columns=names), x="date", y=list(names.values()), color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN],
              labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent change over 12 months", "variable": "Measure"},
              title="All three money measures grew fast at the end of 2008 and in 2009")
fig.update_traces(line_width=2.5)
shade_recessions(fig, "1990-01-01")
fig.add_annotation(x="2019-09-01", y=28.5, text="M1 redefined in May 2020:<br>growth across the break not shown",
                   showarrow=False, xanchor="right", font=dict(size=12))
fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[-15, 31], tickvals=[-10, -5, 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30]), legend_title_text="",
                  legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

Sources. Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, H.6 Money Stock Measures, via FRED: Currency Component of M1 (CURRSL), M1 (M1SL) and M2 (M2SL); recession dates: National Bureau of Economic Research, business cycle dates, as the indicator USREC, via FRED. The 12-month growth rates are our own calculation. Prepared files: data/ch14/fig14-6.csv, data/ch14/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Between October and December 2008, M1 growth jumped from about 7 to about 17 percent and currency growth from 4 to 7 percent; all three measures stayed high for most of 2009. The money supply grew, it did not collapse.
  • M2 grew by up to 27 percent in 2020–2021, with the Covid-19 relief programs, and then fell from late 2022 to early 2024, for the first time since the series began in 1959.
  • Money growth swings a lot from year to year. A single year of fast growth does not mean inflation is coming.

Beyond the United States: broad money growth in 166 economies

Did money collapse anywhere else after 2008? The World Bank’s World Development Indicators report the growth of broad money for most countries: the growth of the end-of-year stock over the previous one. Broad money follows the IMF’s definition: currency plus every kind of deposit, so it is close to M2 but not equal to it (for the United States its growth has a correlation of 0.8 with M2’s December growth, and it even fell in 2010, when M2 grew). The euro-area countries share one money, so the file uses the European Central Bank’s M3 for the euro area instead. The data are annual, from 1990.

Python note. ", ".join(parts) glues a list of texts into one, with a comma between them, and parts[:3] keeps its first three items. rows.empty is true when the filter finds no row, here when a country has no value for 2009.

def money_world_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 6 for other countries: growth of broad money over each year, in percent."""
    data = money_world[money_world.country.isin(countries)]
    if data.empty:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    parts = []
    for name in countries:
        rows = data[(data.country == name) & (data.year == 2009)]
        parts.append(f"{name} no data" if rows.empty else f"{name} {round(rows.broad_money_growth.iloc[0], 1) + 0.0:.1f}%")
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="broad_money_growth", color="country", color_discrete_map=MONEY_COLORS,
                  markers=True, labels={"year": "Year", "broad_money_growth": "Growth over the year (%)",
                                        "country": "Country"},
                  title="Broad money growth in 2009: " + ", ".join(parts[:3]) + (" ..." if len(parts) > 3 else ""))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    y_range = fit_axis(data.broad_money_growth.min(), data.broad_money_growth.max(), [(-15, 31), (-30, 62), (-100, 210)])
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1989, 2026], yaxis_range=y_range, legend_title_text="")
    return fig

Bubbles in stock and home prices

Asset prices that rise far above their long-run averages can fall sharply, and when they do, wealth and spending fall with them. We look at the stock market and at real home prices.

Fig. 7: The price-earnings ratio in the stock market

Goal. Measure stock prices against company profits and look for bubbles.

In standard finance models, a stock is worth the present value of the profits it will earn. Robert Shiller’s price-earnings ratio divides the stock price index by the average real earnings of the previous ten years (it is often called the CAPE). When the ratio climbs far above its long-run average, prices have usually come back down. The textbook marks the average with a dashed line; the slider lets you choose the years behind that average.

Why only the United States? Shiller’s monthly prices and earnings, back to 1871, are free only for the U.S. stock market. Price-earnings ratios of this kind for other markets are compiled by private index firms and are not open data, so this figure stays American.

cape = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-7.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
cape.tail(3)
date cape cape_average
1747 2026-08-01 40.9874 17.8044
1748 2026-09-01 40.5809 17.8044
1749 2026-10-01 40.7106 17.8044

Python note. px.area draws a line and fills the area below it. cape.date.dt.year >= since is true for the months from the year since on. cape.cape.iloc[-1] is the last value of the column.

def cape_chart(since=1881):
    """Fig. 14.7: the price-earnings ratio and its average from the year since to today."""
    recent = cape[cape.date.dt.year >= since]
    average = recent.cape.mean()
    fig = px.area(cape, x="date", y="cape", color_discrete_sequence=["#5aa0d8"],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "cape": "Price-earnings ratio"},
                  title=f"Price-earnings ratio: {cape.cape.iloc[-1]:.1f} in {cape.date.iloc[-1]:%b %Y}; "
                        f"average since {since}: {average:.1f}")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[recent.date.iloc[0], cape.date.iloc[-1]], y=[average, average], mode="lines",
                             name=f"Average since {since}", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2, dash="dash")))
    for year in [1929, 1999]:
        top = cape.loc[cape[cape.date.dt.year == year].cape.idxmax()]
        fig.add_annotation(x=top.date, y=top.cape, text=f"{top.date:%b %Y}: {top.cape:.1f}", ax=-60, ay=-25)
    fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[0, 51], tickvals=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50]), showlegend=False)
    return fig
interact(cape_chart, since=IntSlider(value=1881, min=1881, max=2001, step=10, description="average since", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 7 with a precomputed slider for the start of the average
slider_figure(cape_chart, "since", [1881, 1901, 1951, 1981, 2001], start=1881, label="average since")

Sources. Data: Robert J. Shiller, Online Data (formerly at econ.yale.edu/~shiller/data.htm), cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio (CAPE, P/E10) from the file ie_data.xls. Prepared file: data/ch14/fig14-7.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The ratio peaked in September 1929, just before the crash, and peaked even higher in December 1999, at the top of the dot-com boom. Both times prices then fell a long way.
  • The average over the whole sample is now 17.8 (the textbook’s 17.4 stopped in 2023). The average since 1990 is much higher: whether today’s high ratio is a bubble depends on which “normal” you believe in.
  • In 2026 the ratio is above 40, close to the 1999 record.

Key numbers: two stock market crashes

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 8: Real home prices in the United States

Goal. See how unusual the housing boom of the 2000s was, and how far prices fell.

Shiller’s index of U.S. home prices is divided by the consumer price index, so it measures real home prices: the price of a house in terms of other goods. It is set to 100 in 1953. We use a ratio (log) scale, on which equal percentage changes look equally tall. The menu picks a boom-and-bust episode, and peak_to_trough measures it.

Python note. log_y=True gives a ratio scale. On such an axis, Plotly expects the range in powers of ten: np.log10(80) is the power of ten that gives 80. A dictionary such as EPISODES stores named values, and EPISODES[episode] gets the two dates of one episode. Dropdown shows a menu of choices.

homes = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-8.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).rename(columns={"real_home_price_1953_100": "price"})
EPISODES = {"1970s boom": ("1975-01-01", "1984-12-31"), "1980s boom": ("1985-01-01", "1997-12-31"),
            "2000s bubble": ("2000-01-01", "2015-12-31"), "2020s boom": ("2020-01-01", "2026-12-31")}


def home_prices(episode="2000s bubble"):
    """Fig. 14.8: real home prices on a ratio scale, with the peak and trough of one episode."""
    peak, trough, fall = peak_to_trough(homes, "price", *EPISODES[episode])
    fig = px.line(homes, x="date", y="price", log_y=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "price": "Index, 1953 = 100 (ratio scale)"},
                  title=f"{episode}: real home prices fell {fall:.1f}% from {peak.date:%b %Y} to {trough.date:%b %Y}")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak.date, trough.date], y=[peak.price, trough.price], mode="markers+text",
                             text=["Peak", "Trough"], textposition=["top center", "bottom center"], showlegend=False,
                             marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(220)], tickvals=[80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200])
    return fig

Python note. *EPISODES[episode] unpacks the pair of dates into two separate arguments, start and end.

interact(home_prices, episode=Dropdown(options=list(EPISODES), value="2000s bubble", description="episode", style=WIDE));

              label="episode")

Sources. Data: Robert J. Shiller, Online Data (formerly at econ.yale.edu/~shiller/data.htm), real home price index from the file Fig3-1.xls (since 1987 the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National index, deflated by the BLS consumer price index). Prepared file: data/ch14/fig14-8.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • From 1953 to 2000 real home prices moved within a narrow band, between about 88 and 115. The boom of the 2000s pushed them far above anything seen before.
  • Real prices fell 35.7 percent from the end of 2005 to early 2012, exactly the textbook’s number. Household wealth fell with them, which is the drop in \(\bar{a}\) of Fig. 2.
  • Earlier booms, around 1979 and 1989, were also followed by real declines. After 2020 prices rose again and have eased only a little.

Beyond the United States: real home prices in 58 economies

Shiller’s index is American. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) collects home price indexes from national sources and divides them by consumer prices, so they also measure real home prices. Its index is set to 100 in 2010 and is quarterly. For the United States it tells the same story: real prices fell 38.9 percent from the first quarter of 2006 to the third quarter of 2011 (Shiller: 35.7 percent). The function peak_to_trough from the start of the notebook works on any country’s rows, so the title reports the largest bust after a peak in 2000–2015 among the countries you pick.

The Fed’s balance sheet and forward guidance

With its rate at zero, the Fed used other tools: it bought assets on a large scale, and it told markets how long rates would stay low.

Fig. 9: Financial assets of the Federal Reserve

Goal. See the size and the composition of the Fed’s balance sheet change during the crisis and after.

With the fed funds rate at zero, the Fed bought other assets on a huge scale: mortgage-backed securities and long-term Treasury bonds. This is quantitative easing (QE), done in three rounds after 2008 and again in 2020. The chart stacks the Fed’s assets by type, from the weekly balance sheet (the H.4.1 release).

The textbook reprints a chart of the Cleveland Fed that split Treasuries by purchase program; that chart is no longer published. We split Treasuries by remaining maturity instead: over one year (“long-term”) and within one year (“short-term”). So our long-term layer is not zero before 2009, as it is in the textbook.

assets = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-9.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
assets.tail(3)
date long_term_treasuries mbs_agency_debt short_term_treasuries credit_market_facilities lending_and_other total_assets
1030 2026-09-30 3543.22 1900.44 1020.95 0.0 278.433 6743.03
1031 2026-10-07 3543.46 1900.44 1022.92 0.0 280.740 6747.56
1032 2026-10-14 3543.71 1900.51 1026.84 0.0 284.580 6755.64

All values are in billions of dollars; total_assets is the sum of the five layers.

Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, H.4.1 Factors Affecting Reserve Balances, via FRED: total assets (WALCL); Treasury securities by remaining maturity, e.g. TREAS15, TREAS1T5 and TREAS10Y; mortgage-backed securities (WSHOMCB); agency debt (FEDDT); Commercial Paper Funding Facility (WCPFF). The grouping into five layers is our own. Prepared file: data/ch14/fig14-9.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 14.9 (a Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland chart reprinted there) in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • In late 2008 the Fed first lent directly to banks and to credit markets (the green and dark layers). These loans were repaid within about two years.
  • QE1, QE2 and QE3 then added mortgage-backed securities and long-term Treasuries, step by step, until the balance sheet reached about 4.5 trillion dollars in 2015.
  • The Covid-19 purchases added more than 4 trillion dollars in two years. Since 2022 the Fed has let its holdings run off, to about 6.8 trillion dollars in 2026.

Beyond the United States: central bank balance sheets in 35 economies

Other central banks bought assets too: the European Central Bank (ECB), the Bank of Japan and the Bank of England all ran large QE programs. Dollars, euros and yen cannot be compared directly, so we divide each central bank’s total assets by its country’s GDP. The BIS publishes this ratio, quarterly from 2000. For the United States it matches the Fed’s assets of Fig. 9 divided by U.S. GDP within 1.7 points (6.2 percent of GDP at the end of 2007, 36.9 percent at the peak in 2021). The euro area appears once, for the whole Eurosystem.

What to notice.

  • Add the euro area, Japan and the United Kingdom: every one of them grew its balance sheet far more than the Fed, relative to its economy. At their peaks in 2021, the Eurosystem held assets of 68 percent of GDP, the Bank of England 48 percent and the Bank of Japan 129 percent, against 37 percent for the Fed.
  • The Bank of Japan’s balance sheet was already 21 percent of GDP in 2007, three times the Fed’s: Japan’s experiments with zero rates and asset purchases started a decade earlier.
  • Add Switzerland: its central bank’s assets reached 145 percent of GDP, but for another reason. It bought foreign currency to stop the Swiss franc from rising, so its assets are mostly foreign bonds.

Key numbers: Table 14.1, the Fed’s balance sheet

Table 14.1 of the textbook summarizes the balance sheet in May 2007 and May 2015. The file fed_balance_sheet.csv holds the monthly averages of the weekly H.4.1 data, so we can rebuild the table for any month. Its total is what the H.4.1 calls total factors supplying reserve funds, the total the textbook uses.

sheet = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fed_balance_sheet.csv").set_index("month")


def balance_sheet(month):
    """Table 14.1: the Fed's assets and liabilities in one month, billions of dollars."""
    row = sheet.loc[month]
    items = {"Assets: U.S. Treasuries": row.treasuries, "Assets: Mortgage-backed securities": row.mbs,
             "Assets: Other": row.total - row.treasuries - row.mbs, "Total assets": row.total,
             "Liabilities: Currency": row.currency, "Liabilities: Reserves": row.reserves,
             "Liabilities: Other": row.total - row.currency - row.reserves, "Total liabilities": row.total}
    return pd.Series(items)


table = pd.DataFrame({"May 2007": balance_sheet("2007-05"), "May 2015": balance_sheet("2015-05"),
                      sheet.index[-1]: balance_sheet(sheet.index[-1])})
table.insert(0, "May 2007, textbook", [790, 0, 116, 906, 814, 7, 85, 906])
table.insert(2, "May 2015, textbook", [2460, 1720, 340, 4520, 1360, 2600, 560, 4520])

Our table matches the textbook’s within 11 billion dollars in every cell. The balance sheet grew fivefold, by more than 3.5 trillion dollars, but new currency paid for only about 15 percent of it (the textbook says “less than 15 percent”; its own numbers give 15.1). The rest came from bank reserves: the Fed paid for its purchases by crediting banks’ accounts at the Fed, and the banks kept the money there.

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 10: The fed funds rate: actual and expected

Goal. See how forward guidance changed what financial markets expected of the Fed.

Firms borrow for years, so they care about long-term interest rates, and a long rate is roughly the average of the short rates expected over its life. By announcing how long it would keep rates low, forward guidance, the Fed could lower long rates even with the fed funds rate at zero. In January 2012 it said rates would stay exceptionally low “at least through late 2014”.

Each dashed line is the path of the fed funds rate that markets expected in June of one year. The textbook uses futures contracts, which are not public; we read the expected path off the Treasury yield curve (forward rates), a close proxy that also contains a small term premium. The slider highlights one year’s forecast.

Why only the United States? Fed funds futures exist only for the Fed, and our proxy needs a full curve of yields at five maturities, every month; FRED has it free only for U.S. Treasuries. (The ECB publishes a similar yield curve for the euro area, if you want to try the method on another central bank.)

paths = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-10.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
actual = paths[["date", "fed_funds"]].dropna()
paths[["date", "expected_2009_06"]].dropna()
date expected_2009_06
22 2009-06-30 0.21
25 2009-08-15 0.19
29 2009-11-14 0.51
35 2010-03-31 0.77
48 2010-12-30 1.66
65 2011-12-30 2.70

The June 2009 path starts at the actual rate, 0.21 percent, and climbs to 2.70 percent by the end of 2011, two and a half years later. Each expected_YYYY_06 column holds one such path; the column fed_funds holds the actual monthly rate.

Python note. date.to_period("M") keeps only the month of a date, so two dates of the same month compare equal. if later.empty: checks whether a filter found no rows. path.iloc[-1, 1] picks a cell by position: the last row (-1) of the second column (1).

def realized_rate(day):
    """The actual fed funds rate in the month of day, as text ("not known yet" for future months)."""
    later = actual[actual.date.dt.to_period("M") == day.to_period("M")]
    if later.empty:
        return "not known yet"
    return f"{later.fed_funds.iloc[0]:.2f}%"


def add_expected_path(fig, year, chosen):
    """One market forecast, made in June of year: thick if chosen, faint otherwise."""
    path = paths[["date", f"expected_{year}_06"]].dropna()
    width, color = 1.5, "rgba(127,178,58,0.45)"
    if chosen:
        width, color = 4, GREEN
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=path.date, y=path[f"expected_{year}_06"], mode="lines", name=f"Expected in June {year}",
                             line=dict(color=color, width=width, dash="dash")))
    return path
def expectations_chart(year=2009):
    """Fig. 14.10: the actual fed funds rate and the paths markets expected each June."""
    fig = px.line(actual, x="date", y="fed_funds", color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"date": "Year", "fed_funds": "Percent"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3, name="Actual fed funds rate")
    for y in range(2008, 2027):
        path = add_expected_path(fig, y, y == year)
        if y == year:
            end, expected = path.date.iloc[-1], path.iloc[-1, 1]
    fig.add_vline(x="2012-01-25", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_annotation(x="2012-01-25", y=5.7, text="Jan 2012: the Fed says rates<br>stay low until late 2014", xanchor="left", ax=30, ay=0)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"June {year}: markets expected {expected:.2f}% for {end:%b %Y}; actual: {realized_rate(end)}",
                      showlegend=False, xaxis_range=["2007-07-01", "2029-06-30"], yaxis=dict(range=[-0.3, 6.2],
                      tickvals=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]))
    return fig
interact(expectations_chart, year=IntSlider(value=2009, min=2008, max=2026, step=1, description="forecast made in June",
                                            style=WIDE));

What to notice.

  • From 2009 to 2015 every forecast expected the Fed to raise rates within about two years, and every one was too high: markets kept thinking the Fed was about to tighten.
  • The flattest forecast of those years is June 2012, just after forward guidance began: markets now believed rates would stay low.
  • The forecasts can also miss the other way. In June 2021 markets expected 0.88 percent for the end of 2023; the Fed, fighting inflation, had raised the rate to 5.33 percent.

Key numbers: how wrong were the markets?

The aftermath: a productivity slowdown?

The recovery after 2009 was slow. One possible reason is that total factor productivity has grown more slowly since the mid-2000s.

Fig. 11: U.S. total factor productivity

Goal. Measure the productivity slowdown that may explain the slow recovery after 2008.

Total factor productivity (TFP) is output divided by a weighted combination of capital and labor: the \(\bar{A}\) of the production model. The Bureau of Labor Statistics measures it for the private business sector and for manufacturing. Both indexes are set to 100 in 2009 and drawn on a ratio scale. The average annual growth rate between two years is

\[g = 100 \times \frac{\ln(x_{\text{end}} / x_{\text{start}})}{\text{end} - \text{start}}.\]

Python note. np.log is the natural logarithm. data.set_index("year")[column] makes the years the row labels of a column, so x[2004] is the value of 2004.

tfp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-11.csv")


def growth_rate(data, column, start, end):
    """Average annual growth in percent from year start to year end, 100 ln(x_end / x_start) / (end - start)."""
    x = data.set_index("year")[column]
    return 100 * np.log(x[end] / x[start]) / (end - start)


LAST_PB = tfp.year[tfp.tfp_private_business.notna()].max()      # last year with data, private business
LAST_MFG = tfp.year[tfp.tfp_manufacturing.notna()].max()         # last year with data, manufacturing
print(f"Private business 2004-{LAST_PB}: {growth_rate(tfp, 'tfp_private_business', 2004, LAST_PB):.2f}% a year")
print(f"Manufacturing 2004-{LAST_MFG}: {growth_rate(tfp, 'tfp_manufacturing', 2004, LAST_MFG):.2f}% a year")
Private business 2004-2025: 0.72% a year
Manufacturing 2004-2024: 0.06% a year
def tfp_chart(start=2004):
    """Fig. 14.11: TFP in private business and manufacturing (2009 = 100, ratio scale), growth since start."""
    names = {"tfp_private_business": "Private business sector", "tfp_manufacturing": "Manufacturing"}
    g_pb = growth_rate(tfp, "tfp_private_business", start, LAST_PB)
    g_mfg = growth_rate(tfp, "tfp_manufacturing", start, LAST_MFG)
    fig = px.line(tfp.rename(columns=names), x="year", y=list(names.values()), log_y=True,
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL], labels={"year": "Year", "value": "TFP, 2009 = 100", "variable": "Sector"},
                  title=f"TFP growth since {start}: private business {g_pb:.2f}%, manufacturing {g_mfg:.2f}% a year")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1987, LAST_PB], y=[100, 100], mode="lines", name="2009 level", showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color="#5aa0d8", width=2)))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=LAST_PB, fillcolor=GREEN, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[np.log10(70), np.log10(122)], tickvals=[70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120])
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

What to notice.

  • From 1995 to 2004 TFP grew fast, by more than 1.5 percent a year in private business: the information-technology boom.
  • Since 2004 growth has been much slower: 0.72 percent a year in private business and close to zero in manufacturing. With the textbook’s data (through 2022) the numbers were 0.5 and 0.2 percent. Revisions raised private-business TFP (today’s data give 0.62 percent for 2004–2022), and the strong years since 2022 add the rest.
  • The slowdown began before the financial crisis, so the crisis cannot be its only cause.

Beyond the United States: TFP in 120 countries

The BLS series is American. The Penn World Table (PWT 11.0) measures TFP for 120 countries, for the whole economy and with labor adjusted for schooling, so its U.S. numbers are lower than the BLS’s private-business numbers: 1.19 percent a year in 1995–2004 and 0.39 percent in 2004–2023, against 1.64 and 0.67 for the BLS. The slowdown is the same. PWT’s index equals 1 in 2017; we set it to 100 in 2009, as in the textbook figure.

Python note. base holds one number per country, the 2009 value, with the country names as row labels. tfp_world.country.map(base) looks up each row’s country in base, so every row is divided by its own country’s 2009 value. start in rows.year.values is true when the country has data for the year start. In the title function, growth is a dictionary country → growth rate, and max(growth, key=growth.get) gives the country with the largest value (min the smallest).

base = tfp_world[tfp_world.year == 2009].set_index("country").tfp
tfp_world["tfp_2009"] = 100 * tfp_world.tfp / tfp_world.country.map(base)
tfp_world = tfp_world[tfp_world.year >= 1980]                       # the years of the textbook figure, and more
TFP_COLORS = group_colors(sorted(tfp_world.country.unique()), list(region_groups(tfp_world).values()),
                          {"United States": BLUE})

def tfp_title(data, countries, start):
    """The title of Fig. 11 for other countries: the fastest and slowest TFP growth from start to 2023."""
    growth, missing = {}, []
    for name in countries:
        rows = data[data.country == name]
        if start in rows.year.values:
            growth[name] = round(growth_rate(rows, "tfp_2009", start, 2023), 2) + 0.0   # + 0.0 avoids -0.00
        else:
            missing.append(name)
    title = f"TFP growth {start}–2023:"
    if growth:
        fast, slow = max(growth, key=growth.get), min(growth, key=growth.get)
        title = title + f" {fast} {growth[fast]:.2f}% a year"
        if slow != fast:
            title = title + f", {slow} {growth[slow]:.2f}%"
    if missing:
        title = title + f" (no {start} data: " + ", ".join(missing) + ")"
    return title
def tfp_world_chart(countries=("United States",), start=2004):
    """Fig. 11 for other countries: PWT TFP (2009 = 100, ratio scale) and its growth from start to 2023."""
    data = tfp_world[tfp_world.country.isin(countries)]
    if data.empty:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="tfp_2009", color="country", log_y=True, color_discrete_map=TFP_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "tfp_2009": "TFP, 2009 = 100 (ratio scale)", "country": "Country"},
                  title=tfp_title(data, countries, start))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=2023, fillcolor=GREEN, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    low, high = fit_axis(data.tfp_2009.min(), data.tfp_2009.max(), [(70, 125), (50, 150), (30, 250)])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)], tickvals=[30, 40, 50, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 150, 200, 250])
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[1979, 2024], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

The Great Depression in the short-run model

Finally, we use the same tools on the 1930s: a rate hike by the Fed and a stock market crash, followed by deflation that raised real interest rates.

Fig. 12: The Great Depression in the IS/MP framework

Goal. Rebuild the textbook’s worked exercise on the Great Depression, one shock at a time.

Three things went wrong after 1928, and each moved the economy further below potential:

  1. A to B. Worried about a stock market bubble, the Fed raised interest rates (MP → MP′).
  2. B to C. The bubble burst in October 1929. Lost wealth and uncertainty cut consumption and investment: \(\bar{a}\) fell and the IS curve shifted back to IS′.
  3. C to D. The slump made inflation fall, through the Phillips curve, from about zero to deflation. The Fed kept the nominal rate \(i\) unchanged, so by the Fisher equation \(R = i - \pi\) (equation 8) the real rate rose (MP″).

The function depression_steps follows the three steps with our model functions, and great_depression draws them. Figs. 12 and 13 show the same event in two diagrams, so one function draws both; the diagram buttons switch between them, and the step slider walks from \(A\) to \(D\).

def depression_steps(hike=HIKE, a_crash=A_CRASH, nu=NU):
    """Exercise 2 (Figs. 14.12-14.13): output, real rate and inflation at the points A, B, C and D."""
    pi_0 = 0.0                                    # inflation was about zero in the late 1920s
    i = R_BAR + pi_0 + hike                       # the Fed raises its nominal rate
    R_B = real_rate(i, pi_0)
    Y_C = is_output(R_B, a_crash)                 # the crash shifts the IS curve back
    pi_D = pi_0 + nu * Y_C                        # Phillips curve: the slump at C lowers inflation
    R_D = real_rate(i, pi_D)                      # i stays fixed, so deflation raises the real rate
    rows = [("A", is_output(R_BAR), R_BAR, pi_0), ("B", is_output(R_B), R_B, pi_0),
            ("C", Y_C, R_B, pi_0), ("D", is_output(R_D, a_crash), R_D, pi_D)]
    steps = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["point", "Y", "R", "pi"])
    steps["d_pi"] = nu * steps.Y + 0.0            # the change in inflation (Fig. 14.13); + 0.0 avoids -0.0
    return steps


depression_steps()
point Y R pi d_pi
0 A 0.0 2.0 0.0 0.0
1 B -3.0 5.0 0.0 -1.5
2 C -6.0 5.0 0.0 -3.0
3 D -9.0 8.0 -3.0 -4.5

Python note. reversed(lines) goes through a list from the end, so the newest MP line is drawn first and keeps its label.

DEP_BOX = ([-15.5, 3.5], [-1.5, 12.5])          # Fig. 12 axes: output and the real interest rate
PC_BOX = ([-15.5, 3.5], [-11.5, 2.5])           # Fig. 13 axes: output and the change in inflation
DEP_Y = np.linspace(-15.5, 3.5, 191)            # output levels at which we draw the curves
STEP_NAMES = ["A: the late 1920s", "B: the Fed raises rates", "C: the stock market crash", "D: deflation"]


def draw_depression_ismp(fig, steps, step, a_crash):
    """Fig. 14.12: IS (and IS' from step C on), one MP line per step, and the points up to step."""
    if step >= 2:
        add_curve(fig, DEP_Y, is_rate(DEP_Y, a_crash), "IS′", TEAL, DEP_BOX)
    add_curve(fig, DEP_Y, is_rate(DEP_Y), "IS", FADED_TEAL if step >= 2 else TEAL, DEP_BOX)
    lines = [("MP", steps.R[0], 0), ("MP′", steps.R[1], 1), ("MP″", steps.R[3], 3)]
    for name, R, first in reversed(lines):
        if first <= step:
            color = BLUE if R == steps.R[step] else FADED_BLUE
            add_curve(fig, DEP_Y, np.full_like(DEP_Y, R), name, color, DEP_BOX)
    for s in range(step + 1):
        where = "bottom left" if s == 3 else "top right"          # D stays readable when it meets C
        add_point(fig, steps.Y[s], steps.R[s], steps.point[s], DEP_BOX, where=where)
def draw_depression_phillips(fig, steps, step, nu):
    """Fig. 14.13: the Phillips curve and the points up to step."""
    add_curve(fig, DEP_Y, nu * DEP_Y, "Phillips curve", GREEN, PC_BOX)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    for s in range(step + 1):
        where = "bottom right" if s == 3 else "top right"         # below the Phillips curve, clear of C
        add_point(fig, steps.Y[s], steps.d_pi[s], steps.point[s], PC_BOX, where=where)
    fig.add_annotation(x=3.3, y=-10.5, text="Below the dotted line, next year's<br>inflation is lower than this year's", showarrow=False,
                       xanchor="right", font=dict(size=13))      # bottom right, away from the curve


def great_depression(step=3, hike=HIKE, a_crash=A_CRASH, nu=NU, diagram="IS/MP"):
    """Figs. 14.12 and 14.13: the Great Depression step by step, in the IS/MP or the Phillips curve diagram."""
    steps = depression_steps(hike, a_crash, nu)
    now = steps.loc[step]
    fig = model_figure()
    if diagram == "IS/MP":
        draw_depression_ismp(fig, steps, step, a_crash)
        title = f"{STEP_NAMES[step]}: Ỹ = {now.Y:.1f}%, R = {now.R:.1f}%, π = {now.pi:.1f}%"
        model_axes(fig, title, DEP_BOX, "Real interest rate, R (%)", [-15, -12, -9, -6, -3, 0, 3], [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
    else:
        draw_depression_phillips(fig, steps, step, nu)
        title = f"{STEP_NAMES[step]}: Ỹ = {now.Y:.1f}%, change in inflation Δπ = {now.d_pi:.1f} points"
        model_axes(fig, title, PC_BOX, "Change in inflation, Δπ (points)", [-15, -12, -9, -6, -3, 0, 3], [-10, -8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2])
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 14.12 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed. The numbers follow the textbook’s worked exercise on the Great Depression.

What to notice.

  • Each step costs 3 percent of output: \(-3\) at \(B\), \(-6\) at \(C\) and \(-9\) at \(D\), the textbook’s example numbers.
  • The third step is the dangerous one. At \(D\) output is even lower, so inflation falls again, the real rate rises again, and so on: a deflationary spiral (equation 11). Nothing in the model stops it unless policy changes.
  • Set \(\bar{\nu} = 0\) (prices that never react): \(D\) coincides with \(C\). The spiral needs prices that fall in a slump.

Fig. 13: The Phillips curve and the Great Depression

Goal. See why the slump turned into deflation, in the Phillips curve diagram.

The Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) says that inflation falls whenever output is below potential. Every point \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) of Fig. 12 lies below potential, so at each of them inflation falls, by more the deeper the slump. Inflation was about zero in the late 1920s, so falling inflation meant deflation: prices fell by about a quarter between 1929 and 1933.

What to notice.

  • With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), inflation falls by 1.5 points a year at \(B\), 3 points at \(C\) and 4.5 points at \(D\).
  • The change in inflation at \(C\) is what raises the real rate from \(C\) to \(D\) in Fig. 12; the even larger fall at \(D\) would push the real rate up once more.
  • A steeper Phillips curve (a larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) makes deflation, and so the spiral, faster.

# Your turn: try it here

Concluding remarks

  • A financial friction \(\bar{f}\) sits between the fed funds rate and the rate at which firms and households borrow, \(R = R^{ff} + \bar{f}\) (equation 1). In 2008 the spread of corporate over Treasury bonds tripled, so the Fed’s cuts did not lower borrowing costs. In the new AD curve, equation (4), the friction acts like a negative demand shock, \(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}\): output falls at first, and inflation drifts down to the lower long-run rate of equation (6), closing a fixed share of the gap each year (equation 7).
  • At the zero lower bound the nominal rate cannot be cut further, which caps reachable output (equation 10), and deflation then raises the real interest rate (the Fisher equation, equation 8). A recession lowers inflation, deflation deepens the recession: a deflationary spiral, equation (11), as in the Great Depression.
  • Leverage turns small falls in asset prices into large losses of net worth (equation 12), which is why higher capital requirements are the core of financial reform.
  • The Fed answered the crisis with zero rates, a fivefold and later tenfold larger balance sheet (quantitative easing) and forward guidance; money growth stayed high, unlike in the 1930s.
  • The data also show the bubbles behind the crisis (stock and home prices), and a slow aftermath: much of the closing of the output gap came from a lower estimate of potential GDP, and TFP growth has been slow since 2004.
  • The next chapter looks at DSGE models, the modern models of business cycles that researchers built on these lessons.

Practice problems

Conceptual problems apply the chapter’s equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to its data files, and modeling problems use its diagrams to answer policy questions; each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge. Try each problem on your own before you open its Hint and its Solution. The sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems

Problem 1 (Basic): How thin was Wall Street’s cushion? At the end of 2007 the investment bank Bear Stearns had $11.8 billion of equity (its net worth) and $383.6 billion of liabilities, according to the report of the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission (pages xix–xx).

  1. Compute its leverage \(\lambda\) and its capital ratio \(\kappa\), as defined in the Model overview.

  2. Use equation (12). What share of its net worth would a 1 percent fall in the value of its assets wipe out? How large a fall would make it insolvent?

  3. The same report says that the five big investment banks had leverage ratios “as high as 40 to 1”, that is $40 of assets for each $1 of capital, so that “less than a 3% drop in asset values could wipe out a firm”. Check this claim with equation (12). Careful: “40 to 1” compares assets with capital, while our \(\lambda\) compares liabilities with net worth.

Hint

Assets are liabilities plus net worth. Then \(\kappa\) is net worth divided by assets, and \(\lambda\) is liabilities divided by net worth. A firm is insolvent once the fall in its net worth reaches 100 percent.

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Assets are \(383.6 + 11.8 = 395.4\) billion dollars, so

\[\lambda = \frac{383.6}{11.8} = 32.5, \qquad \kappa = \frac{11.8}{395.4} = 0.030,\]

a capital ratio of 3.0 percent. As a check, \(\kappa = 1/(1 + \lambda) = 1/33.5 = 0.030\).

(b) By equation (12), net worth changes by \(-(1 + \lambda)\,x\) percent when assets lose \(x\) percent. A fall of \(x = 1\) percent destroys \(33.5 \times 1 = 33.5\) percent of net worth, a third of it. Net worth reaches zero when \((1 + \lambda)\,x = 100\), that is at \(x = 100/33.5 = 3.0\) percent, which is \(\kappa\) itself. A fall of 3 percent in the value of its assets was enough to make Bear Stearns insolvent.

(c) Assets divided by capital is \(1 + \lambda = 40\), so \(\lambda = 39\) and \(\kappa = 1/40 = 0.025\). By equation (12) the firm is wiped out when its assets lose \(x = \kappa = 2.5\) percent, which is indeed “less than 3%”. A 1 percent fall already costs \(40 \times 1 = 40\) percent of net worth.

Interpretation. Real home prices fell 35.7 percent from 2005 to 2012 (Fig. 8). With cushions of 2.5 to 3 percent, losses on even a small part of a bank’s mortgage-related assets could make lenders doubt that it was still solvent. That doubt is what raises the risk premium \(\bar{f}\) in equation (1).

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Why did stock prices fall in 2022? To fight inflation, the Fed raised its rate quickly in 2022: in our data (Fig. 10) the fed funds rate went from 0.08 percent in December 2021 to 4.10 percent in December 2022. Over the same year, Shiller’s price-earnings ratio (Fig. 7) fell from 38.3 to 28.3, and the 10-year Treasury yield (Fig. 1) rose from 1.47 to 3.62 percent. Treat Shiller’s ratio as the \(P/E\) of equation (13).

  1. What value of \(R - g\) does equation (13) imply in December 2021 and in December 2022? By how many points did it rise?

  2. Suppose instead that the whole rise in the 10-year yield had gone into the discount rate \(R\), with \(g\) unchanged. What price-earnings ratio would equation (13) predict for December 2022? Compare it with the actual 28.3.

  3. Give one economic reason why the ratio fell less than in (b).

Hint

Turn equation (13) around: \(R - g = 1/(P/E)\), as a fraction; multiply by 100 to get percent. For (b), add the rise in the yield to the \(R - g\) of December 2021, then invert again.

Your answer:

Solution

(a) From equation (13), \(R - g = 1/(P/E)\):

\[\text{December 2021: } R - g = \frac{1}{38.3} = 0.0261, \qquad \text{December 2022: } R - g = \frac{1}{28.3} = 0.0353,\]

that is 2.61 and 3.53 percent: a rise of 0.92 points.

(b) The yield rose by \(3.62 - 1.47 = 2.15\) points. Then \(R - g = 2.61 + 2.15 = 4.76\) percent, and

\[\frac{P}{E} = \frac{1}{0.0476} = 21.0,\]

a fall of 45 percent from 38.3. The actual ratio fell by only 26 percent, to 28.3.

(c) Any one of these is a good answer:

  • The 10-year yield is a nominal rate. Part of its rise came from higher expected inflation, which also raises the expected growth of profits in dollars, \(g\). So \(R - g\) rose by less than the yield.
  • Investors may have asked for a smaller extra return for holding stocks rather than safe bonds, which lowers \(R\).
  • Shiller’s ratio divides by ten years of past earnings, not by next year’s profits, so it is only a rough version of the \(P/E\) in equation (13).

The general lesson of equation (13) holds either way: when \(R - g\) is small, prices are very sensitive to it. A rise of less than one point in \(R - g\) cut the ratio by about a quarter.

Problem 3 (Challenge): What does the AD curve look like at the zero lower bound? The new AD curve (4) assumes that the central bank can always follow its rule. In 2009 the Fed could not: in our data (Fig. 4) the Taylor rule with \(\bar{r} = 2\) called for nominal rates of −0.26 and −0.48 percent in the second and third quarters, while the fed funds rate stayed at 0.18 and 0.16 percent. Derive what happens to the AD curve when the rule hits the floor. Use the baseline (\(\bar{r} = \bar{\pi} = 2\), \(\bar{b} = \bar{m} = 1\), \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\)) and the 2008 shocks (\(\bar{a} = -2\), \(\bar{f} = 4\)).

  1. Use equation (9) with \(\bar{x} = 0\) to find the inflation rate \(\pi_k\) below which the rule asks for a negative nominal rate. What is \(\pi_k\) in the baseline?

  2. Below \(\pi_k\) the nominal rate stays at zero. Show that output is then \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} + \bar{b}\,(\bar{r} + \pi_t)\), as in equation (10), and explain why this part of the AD curve slopes upward in a diagram with inflation on the vertical axis.

  3. Combine this branch with the AS curve \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) and solve for \(\tilde{Y}_t\). In Fig. 3, inflation is 0 percent in period 1. Compute output and inflation in period 2, and compare them with the path of Fig. 3 (output −2.7 percent, inflation −1.3 percent).

  4. Compute period 3. What does the result say about point \(C\) of Fig. 3?

Hint
  1. Set \(i^{ff}_t = 0\) in equation (9) and solve for \(\pi_t\). (b) With a zero nominal rate, the Fisher equation gives \(R^{ff}_t = -\pi_t\); then use equation (1) and the IS curve. (c) Replace \(\pi_t\) by the AS curve, collect the \(\tilde{Y}_t\) terms on the left as in Step 3 of the AS/AD block, and divide by \(1 - \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\).

Your answer:

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) With \(\bar{x} = 0\), equation (9) is \(i^{ff}_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\). Set it to zero and collect the \(\pi_t\) terms:

\[0 = \bar{r} + (1 + \bar{m})\,\pi_t - \bar{m}\bar{\pi} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_k = \frac{\bar{m}\bar{\pi} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{m}}.\]

In the baseline \(\pi_k = (2 - 2)/2 = 0\): the rule needs a negative nominal rate as soon as inflation turns negative.

(b) At \(i^{ff}_t = 0\) the real fed funds rate is \(R^{ff}_t = 0 - \pi_t\), so firms pay \(R_t = \bar{f} - \pi_t\) by equation (1). Put this into the IS curve:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(\bar{f} - \pi_t - \bar{r}) = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} + \bar{b}\,(\bar{r} + \pi_t).\]

Now \(\partial\tilde{Y}_t/\partial\pi_t = +\bar{b} > 0\). Solved for inflation, \(\pi_t = (\tilde{Y}_t - \bar{a} + \bar{b}\bar{f})/\bar{b} - \bar{r}\), a line with the positive slope \(1/\bar{b}\). On the normal branch, lower inflation makes the central bank cut its rate, and output rises. On this branch the nominal rate cannot fall, so lower inflation raises the real rate, and output falls. The two branches meet at the kink: at \(\pi_t = 0\) both give \(\tilde{Y}_t = -6 + 2 = -4\) percent.

(c) Replace \(\pi_t\) by \(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) and collect the \(\tilde{Y}_t\) terms:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} + \bar{b}\bar{r} + \bar{b}\pi_{t-1} + \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} + \bar{b}\,(\bar{r} + \pi_{t-1})}{1 - \bar{b}\bar{\nu}}.\]

In period 1 the rule asks for \(i^{ff} = 2\pi_1 = 0\), exactly the floor, so Fig. 3 is still right. In period 2, with \(\pi_1 = 0\):

\[\tilde{Y}_2 = \frac{-2 - 4 + 1 \times (2 + 0)}{1 - 0.5} = \frac{-4}{0.5} = -8 \text{ percent}, \qquad \pi_2 = 0 + 0.5 \times (-8) = -4 \text{ percent}.\]

The recession is three times as deep as in Fig. 3 (−2.7 percent), and inflation falls three times as far. The factor \(1/(1 - \bar{b}\bar{\nu}) = 2\) is an amplifier: lower output lowers inflation, which raises the real rate and lowers output again.

(d) Period 3: \(\tilde{Y}_3 = (-6 + 2 - 4)/0.5 = -16\) percent and \(\pi_3 = -4 + 0.5 \times (-16) = -12\) percent. Subtracting the formula of (c) for two periods in a row gives \(\tilde{Y}_t - \tilde{Y}_{t-1} = \bar{b}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_{t-2})/(1 - \bar{b}\bar{\nu}) = \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_{t-1}/(1 - \bar{b}\bar{\nu})\), so \(\tilde{Y}_t = \tilde{Y}_{t-1}/(1 - \bar{b}\bar{\nu})\): the gap doubles every period. This is a deflationary spiral, like equation (11), only faster, because here the real rate reacts to this period’s inflation. Point \(C\) of Fig. 3, with output at potential and inflation at −4 percent, can never be reached: there the rule would need a nominal rate of \(2 \times (-4) = -8\) percent. That is why the IS/MP diagram is the better tool at the zero lower bound, and why policy then needs tools that raise \(\bar{a}\), lower \(\bar{f}\) or raise expected inflation.

A check with the notebook’s functions:

pi_prev = 0.0                                  # inflation in period 1 of Fig. 3
for t in [2, 3]:
    Y = (A_HOUSING - B_BAR * F_CRISIS + B_BAR * (R_BAR + pi_prev)) / (1 - B_BAR * NU)
    pi = as_inflation(Y, pi_prev)
    print(f"Period {t}: Y~ = {Y:.1f}%, pi = {pi:.1f}%, equation (10) at this pi: "
          f"{zlb_best_output(pi, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS):.1f}%")
    pi_prev = pi
print(f"Fig. 3, period 2: Y~ = {crisis_path().Y[2]:.1f}%, pi = {crisis_path().pi[2]:.1f}%")
