Data-based problems

Problem 4 (Basic): Did “whatever it takes” work? On 26 July 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, the President of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, said in a speech in London that “within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro”. Use sovereign_spreads.csv, the spreads over Germany of the 10-year government bond yields compiled by the OECD (long-term interest rates, via FRED).

  1. What were the spreads of Italy and Spain in July 2012 and in July 2013?

  2. Of Greece, Ireland, Italy, Portugal and Spain, whose spread fell the most from July 2012 to July 2013, in points and in percent?

Hint

Monthly dates are the first day of the month, so July 2012 is "2012-07-01". Write a loop over the five names. Inside it, keep the rows of one country and pick the value of spread_germany on each date with .iloc[0].

# Your answer here
Solution

Read the file, then loop over the five countries and print both values, the change in points and the change in percent:

spreads_eu = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "sovereign_spreads.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
for name in ["Greece", "Ireland", "Italy", "Portugal", "Spain"]:
    rows = spreads_eu[spreads_eu.country == name]
    before = rows[rows.date == "2012-07-01"].spread_germany.iloc[0]
    after = rows[rows.date == "2013-07-01"].spread_germany.iloc[0]
    print(f"{name}: {before:.2f} -> {after:.2f} points, change {after - before:+.2f} ({100 * (after / before - 1):.0f}%)")
Greece: 24.58 -> 8.96 points, change -15.61 (-64%)
Ireland: 4.88 -> 2.31 points, change -2.56 (-53%)
Italy: 4.75 -> 2.85 points, change -1.90 (-40%)
Portugal: 9.25 -> 5.30 points, change -3.94 (-43%)
Spain: 5.55 -> 3.10 points, change -2.46 (-44%)

(a) Italy’s spread fell from 4.75 to 2.85 points and Spain’s from 5.55 to 3.10 points.

(b) Greece’s spread fell the most, by 15.61 points or 64 percent. Of the other four, Portugal fell most in points, by 3.94, and Ireland most in percent, by 53 percent. Every spread fell by at least 40 percent within a year. These spreads are the risk premium that markets charged each government on top of what Germany paid, the euro-area version of \(\bar{f}\) in equation (1). Be careful with the cause, though: many things changed in that year, and a before-and-after comparison cannot prove that the speech alone brought the spreads down.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): How much of the Fed’s balance sheet has been unwound? From 2022 the Fed let its holdings of bonds shrink, and on 29 October 2025 it announced that it would stop reducing its securities holdings on December 1. Use fig14-9.csv, the Fed’s weekly assets from its H.4.1 release, via FRED (WALCL), and fed_balance_sheet.csv, the monthly averages of the same H.4.1 release.

  1. When did total assets peak, and at what level?

  2. What was the lowest level after the peak, and in which week? Does the date fit the Fed’s announcement?

  3. Take 11 March 2020, the last week before the jump of March 2020 in our data, as the start of the Covid-19 expansion. What share of the rise from then to the peak had been reversed at the low point?

  4. In fed_balance_sheet.csv, compare April 2022 with December 2025. How much did the total, currency and reserves change? The other liabilities, total - currency - reserves, include the Treasury’s account at the Fed and reverse repurchase agreements. Which liability fell the most?

Hint

.idxmax() gives the row of the peak. For the low point, keep only the weeks from the peak on and use .idxmin(). In fed_balance_sheet.csv the months are text such as "2022-04", so after .set_index("month") you can pick a month with .loc["2022-04"], and subtract one month’s row from another’s.

# Your answer here
Solution

First the weekly data: the peak, the lowest week after it, and the share of the expansion reversed.

fed_assets = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-9.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
top = fed_assets.loc[fed_assets.total_assets.idxmax()]
later = fed_assets[fed_assets.date >= top.date]
low = later.loc[later.total_assets.idxmin()]
start = fed_assets[fed_assets.date == "2020-03-11"].total_assets.iloc[0]
share = 100 * (top.total_assets - low.total_assets) / (top.total_assets - start)
print(f"Peak: {top.total_assets:,.0f} billion on {top.date:%d %b %Y}")
print(f"Low after the peak: {low.total_assets:,.0f} billion on {low.date:%d %b %Y}")
print(f"11 Mar 2020: {start:,.0f} billion; share of the expansion reversed: {share:.1f}%")
Peak: 8,965 billion on 13 Apr 2022
Low after the peak: 6,536 billion on 03 Dec 2025
11 Mar 2020: 4,312 billion; share of the expansion reversed: 52.2%

Then the monthly balance sheet, liabilities side:

months = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fed_balance_sheet.csv").set_index("month")
months["other"] = months.total - months.currency - months.reserves
change = months.loc["2025-12"] - months.loc["2022-04"]
print(change[["total", "currency", "reserves", "other"]].round(0))
total      -2377.0
currency     163.0
reserves    -650.0
other      -1889.0
dtype: float64

(a) Total assets peaked at 8,965 billion dollars in the week of 13 April 2022.

(b) The lowest level after the peak was 6,536 billion dollars, on 3 December 2025, the first Wednesday after December 1: it fits the announcement. Since then total assets have grown again.

(c) About half: 52.2 percent of the Covid-19 expansion had been reversed.

(d) From April 2022 to December 2025 the total fell by 2,377 billion dollars. Liabilities must fall by as much as assets, and most of the fall, 1,889 billion, came from the other liabilities. Reserves fell by only 650 billion, and currency even grew by 163 billion. Quantitative tightening mostly drained the other liabilities, while banks kept about 2.9 trillion dollars of reserves at the Fed.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): Is the productivity slowdown global? Fig. 11 showed that U.S. TFP growth slowed around 2004, before the financial crisis. Did the rest of the world slow down too? Use TFP from the Penn World Table 11.0 in tfp_world.csv and the notebook’s function growth_rate, and stop in 2019, before Covid-19.

  1. For the G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States), compute average TFP growth over 1995–2004 and 2004–2019. How many of the seven slowed down?

  2. Do the same for all 120 countries. How many slowed down, and what were the median growth rates in the two periods?

  3. Which five countries slowed down the most? Does their slowdown look like a story about technology?

Hint

growth_rate(data, "tfp", 1995, 2004) works on the rows of one country. Read the file into a table, loop over its .country.unique(), append one dictionary per country to a list, and turn the list into a DataFrame. Then .median() and .sort_values() do the rest.

# Your answer here
Solution

One loop computes both growth rates for every country; the rest are simple summaries.

tfp_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "tfp_world.csv")
rows = []
for name in tfp_all.country.unique():
    data = tfp_all[tfp_all.country == name]
    rows.append({"country": name, "before": growth_rate(data, "tfp", 1995, 2004),
                 "after": growth_rate(data, "tfp", 2004, 2019)})
slow = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("country")
slow["change"] = slow.after - slow.before
g7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]
print(slow.loc[g7].round(2) + 0.0)                 # + 0.0 turns a rounded -0.00 into 0.00
print(f"Slower after 2004: {(slow.change < 0).sum()} of {len(slow)} countries")
print(f"Median growth: {slow.before.median():.2f}% (1995-2004), {slow.after.median():.2f}% (2004-2019)")
print(slow.sort_values("change").head(5).round(2))
                before  after  change
country                              
Canada            0.41  -0.05   -0.46
France            0.73  -0.19   -0.92
Germany           0.44   0.43    0.00
Italy            -0.63  -0.85   -0.23
Japan             0.01   0.07    0.06
United Kingdom    0.93  -0.15   -1.09
United States     1.19   0.30   -0.89
Slower after 2004: 74 of 120 countries
Median growth: 0.44% (1995-2004), 0.20% (2004-2019)
                     before  after  change
country                                   
Iraq                  10.67  -0.92  -11.59
Armenia               10.51   2.83   -7.68
Kuwait                 1.15  -5.81   -6.95
Trinidad and Tobago    4.64  -1.66   -6.31
Qatar                  0.10  -5.41   -5.51

(a) Six of the seven grew more slowly after 2004, but Germany only by less than 0.01 point (its rounded change is 0.00): its growth stayed at 0.4 percent a year. So five clearly slowed down: Canada, France, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States, with the largest slowdowns in the United Kingdom (1.09 points), France (0.92) and the United States (0.89). Japan sped up a little, from almost zero (0.01 to 0.07 percent a year).

(b) In 74 of the 120 countries (62 percent) TFP grew more slowly in 2004–2019 than in 1995–2004, and the median growth rate fell from 0.44 to 0.20 percent a year. The slowdown is broad, not only American, so a purely American cause, or the U.S. financial crisis alone, cannot explain it.

(c) Iraq, Armenia, Kuwait, Trinidad and Tobago and Qatar. Iraq and Armenia had TFP growth above 10 percent a year in 1995–2004, far outside the normal range, so their “slowdown” is mostly the end of an unusual boom. Kuwait, Qatar and Trinidad and Tobago are oil and gas exporters, whose measured TFP moves with oil output and prices, as the notebook noted for Kuwait and Saudi Arabia under Fig. 11. None of the five is a story about the technology frontier: look at your data before you read a TFP number as technology.

Problem 7 (Challenge): Too low for too long, around the world? Taylor (2007) argued that from 2002 to 2005 the Fed kept its rate well below what his rule recommended, and that this may have helped cause the boom and bust in housing. Bernanke (2010) answered with evidence from 20 industrial countries: the stance of monetary policy relative to the Taylor rule explained only about 5 percent of the differences in real house-price growth between the fourth quarter of 2001 and the third quarter of 2006. Test the debate with our data: taylor_world.csv (policy rates from the BIS; inflation and output gaps from the OECD Economic Outlook) and house_prices_world.csv (real home prices from the BIS).

  1. For each of the 14 central banks, compute the average over 2002–2006 of the Taylor rule minus the policy rate. Use the notebook’s taylor_rule, with core inflation where it exists and headline inflation otherwise, as in Fig. 4. Then compute the growth of real home prices from 2001Q4 to 2006Q3, in percent. Keep the economies that have both numbers.

  2. Compute the correlation between the two, and its square: the share of the differences in house-price growth that the policy gap “explains”. Compare it with Bernanke’s 5 percent.

  3. Drop Israel and compute the correlation again. What does this tell you about a correlation from about ten points?

  4. All euro-area countries faced the same ECB rate. Compare the growth of real home prices over the same quarters in Germany and Spain. What does this suggest about the causes of housing booms?

Hint

Add a column gap = taylor_rule(inflation, output_gap) - policy_rate. Quarters are dated by their first day, so 2001Q4 is "2001-10-01" and 2006Q3 is "2006-07-01". In a loop over the central banks, skip an economy when one of its numbers is missing: Japan has no policy rate for 2002–2006, and Czechia and Poland have no home prices for 2001.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) and (b) Build the policy gap, then loop over the central banks:

rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "taylor_world.csv")
rates["inflation"] = rates.core_inflation.fillna(rates.headline_inflation)
rates["gap"] = taylor_rule(rates.inflation, rates.output_gap) - rates.policy_rate
houses = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "house_prices_world.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
rows = []
for name in rates.country.unique():
    boom = rates[(rates.country == name) & (rates.year >= 2002) & (rates.year <= 2006)].gap.mean()
    start = houses[(houses.country == name) & (houses.date == "2001-10-01")].real_price
    end = houses[(houses.country == name) & (houses.date == "2006-07-01")].real_price
    if len(start) == 1 and len(end) == 1 and not np.isnan(boom):
        rows.append({"country": name, "policy_gap": boom, "house_growth": 100 * (end.iloc[0] / start.iloc[0] - 1)})
both = pd.DataFrame(rows)
r = both.policy_gap.corr(both.house_growth)
print(both.sort_values("policy_gap").round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(f"{len(both)} economies: correlation {r:.2f}, squared {r ** 2:.2f}")
       country  policy_gap  house_growth
        Israel        -3.3          -9.0
        Norway        -1.4          35.5
   New Zealand        -0.8          69.9
United Kingdom        -0.4          58.6
        Sweden        -0.2          46.0
     Australia         0.4          34.5
   Switzerland         0.6          12.8
   South Korea         1.3          13.6
     Euro area         1.4          23.9
 United States         1.6          40.6
        Canada         2.1          44.5
11 economies: correlation 0.22, squared 0.05

Eleven economies have both numbers. The correlation is 0.22: looser policy (a positive gap) goes with somewhat faster growth of home prices, the sign Taylor expected. But its square is 0.05, so the policy gap “explains” only 5 percent of the differences in house-price growth, just like Bernanke’s estimate. New Zealand and the United Kingdom had policy slightly tighter than the rule and some of the largest booms (70 and 59 percent), while the United States, with the second-loosest policy, had a boom of 41 percent.

(c) Without Israel:

others = both[both.country != "Israel"]
print(f"Without Israel: correlation {others.policy_gap.corr(others.house_growth):.2f}")
Without Israel: correlation -0.44

The sign flips: without Israel, looser policy goes with slower house-price growth. Israel is unusual: in our data it kept its policy rate above 7 percent in 2002–2003 while core inflation fell from 6.0 to −0.3 percent, and its real home prices fell. One economy decides the sign. With about ten points, a correlation can swing with a single observation, so this simple test cannot settle the debate either way; that would take more countries, more years and other explanations held constant.

(d) Germany and Spain:

for name in ["Germany", "Spain"]:
    start = houses[(houses.country == name) & (houses.date == "2001-10-01")].real_price.iloc[0]
    end = houses[(houses.country == name) & (houses.date == "2006-07-01")].real_price.iloc[0]
    print(f"{name}: real home prices {100 * (end / start - 1):+.1f}%")
Germany: real home prices -9.4%
Spain: real home prices +71.3%

Under the same policy rate, real home prices fell 9.4 percent in Germany and rose 71.3 percent in Spain. Something other than the central bank’s rate must explain most of the difference: local demand and supply, lending standards, or money flowing in from abroad, the capital inflows that Bernanke pointed to in the same speech. Within a monetary union, no single ECB rate could have suited both countries.

Modeling problems

Problem 8 (Basic): How much output did the bank rescue buy? In October 2008 Congress authorized $700 billion for the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), and about $250 billion of it was committed to programs that stabilized banks. In the model, a successful rescue lowers the financial friction \(\bar{f}\). Measure \(\bar{f}\) as the BAA spread of Fig. 1 minus its 1996–2007 average of 2.16 points: that gives 3.85 points in December 2008 and 0.62 points in December 2009.

  1. Keep the housing shock at \(\bar{a}' = -2\) and the Fed’s cut of Fig. 2. Set the friction slider below to each month’s value, rounded to the nearest half point, and read output at \(D\).

  2. By how much did output at \(D\) rise between the two months? Confirm with is_output and borrowing_rate, using the unrounded values.

Hint

In panel (b) of the chart, \(D\) is where the line MP″, at \(R = R^{ff} + \bar{f}\), meets IS′, and the title reports its output. In code, the Fed’s rate after its cut is R_BAR + A_HOUSING / B_BAR.

interact(housing_crisis, a_new=fixed(-2.0),
         f=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="financial friction f̄ (points)", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 2 above, adapted from Fig. 14.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) At \(\bar{f} = 4\) (December 2008) the title shows \(R = 4.0\) percent and output at \(D\) of −4.0 percent. At \(\bar{f} = 0.5\) (December 2009) it shows \(R = 0.5\) percent and output at \(D\) of −0.5 percent.

(b) With the Fed’s rate fixed at \(R^{ff} = \bar{r} + \bar{a}'/\bar{b} = 0\) percent, output at \(D\) is

\[\tilde{Y} = \bar{a}' - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff} + \bar{f} - \bar{r}) = -2 - 1 \times (0 + \bar{f} - 2) = -\bar{b}\bar{f},\]

so every point taken off the premium adds \(\bar{b} = 1\) point of output. With the unrounded values:

R_ff = R_BAR + A_HOUSING / B_BAR                 # the Fed's cut of Fig. 2: 0 percent
for month, f in [("December 2008", 3.85), ("December 2009", 0.62)]:
    print(f"{month}: f = {f:.2f}, output at D = {is_output(borrowing_rate(R_ff, f), A_HOUSING):.2f}%")
December 2008: f = 3.85, output at D = -3.85%
December 2009: f = 0.62, output at D = -0.62%

Output at \(D\) rises by \(3.85 - 0.62 = 3.23\) points (3.5 points with the rounded slider values), exactly the fall of the spread from 6.01 to 2.78 points in our data.

Policy answer. In this diagram, lowering the friction is worth as much as cutting the Fed’s rate by the same amount, and in 2009 the Fed’s rate could not go much lower. But the model cannot say how much of the fall in the spread came from TARP: the Fed’s lending to banks and markets (Fig. 9) and the start of the recovery lowered it too.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): Should the central bank react more strongly to inflation? Imagine a debate at a central bank (a hypothetical one): a board member argues that a more aggressive rule, \(\bar{m} = 2\) instead of 1, would make a crisis like that of 2008 short and mild. Test the claim in the AS/AD model of Fig. 3, with the 2008 shocks (\(\bar{a} = -2\), \(\bar{f} = 4\)) held fixed.

  1. For \(\bar{m} = 1\) and \(\bar{m} = 2\), read output and inflation in period 1, and long-run inflation at \(C\).

  2. In which period does output first come within 1 percent of potential? Then use crisis_path to add up the output gaps of the 15 periods, a measure of the total loss.

  3. Use equation (9) with \(\bar{x} = 0\) to compute the nominal rate the rule asks for in period 1 under each \(\bar{m}\). Can the central bank deliver it? What does this mean for the board member’s claim?

Hint

Move the period slider: the title shows that period’s output and inflation, and long-run inflation at \(C\). In code, crisis_path(m=2.0) gives the whole path, and path.Y[1:] are the periods after the shock. Equation (9) with \(\bar{x} = 0\) reads \(i = \bar{r} + \pi + \bar{m}\,(\pi - \bar{\pi})\).

interact(crisis_asad,
         t=IntSlider(value=1, min=1, max=15, step=1, description="period t", style=WIDE),
         a=fixed(-2.0), f=fixed(4.0),
         m=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=1.0, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 3 above, adapted from Fig. 14.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) With \(\bar{m} = 1\) the title shows output of −4.0 percent and inflation of 0.0 percent in period 1, and \(\pi_C = -4.0\) percent. With \(\bar{m} = 2\), equation (5) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -6/(1 + 1 \times 2 \times 0.5) = -3.0\) percent and \(\pi_1 = 2 + 0.5 \times (-3) = 0.5\) percent, and equation (6) gives \(\pi_C = 2 - 6/2 = -1.0\) percent.

(b) By equation (7) the gap left each period is the share \(1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\): 2/3 with \(\bar{m} = 1\) and 1/2 with \(\bar{m} = 2\).

for m in [1.0, 2.0]:
    path = crisis_path(m=m)
    close = path[(path.period >= 1) & (path.Y.abs() < 1)].period.iloc[0]
    pi_C = PI_BAR + (A_HOUSING - B_BAR * F_CRISIS) / (B_BAR * m)          # equation (6)
    i_1 = R_BAR + path.pi[1] + m * (path.pi[1] - PI_BAR)                 # equation (9) with x = 0
    print(f"m = {m:.0f}: Y1 = {path.Y[1]:.2f}%, pi1 = {path.pi[1]:.2f}%, pi_C = {pi_C:.2f}%, "
          f"within 1% in period {close}, total {path.Y[1:].sum():.2f}, i in period 1 = {i_1:+.2f}%")
m = 1: Y1 = -4.00%, pi1 = 0.00%, pi_C = -4.00%, within 1% in period 5, total -11.97, i in period 1 = +0.00%
m = 2: Y1 = -3.00%, pi1 = 0.50%, pi_C = -1.00%, within 1% in period 3, total -6.00, i in period 1 = -0.50%

Output first comes within 1 percent of potential in period 5 with \(\bar{m} = 1\) and in period 3 with \(\bar{m} = 2\), and the total loss halves, from about 12 to 6 percent of a year’s potential output. There is a neat reason. The AS curve says \(\tilde{Y}_t = (\pi_t - \pi_{t-1})/\bar{\nu}\), so the sum of the gaps telescopes:

\[\sum_{t \geq 1} \tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\pi_C - \pi_0}{\bar{\nu}} = \frac{-6}{0.5} = -12 \;\;(\bar{m} = 1), \qquad \frac{-3}{0.5} = -6 \;\;(\bar{m} = 2).\]

Each point of lasting disinflation costs \(1/\bar{\nu} = 2\) points of output, and the aggressive rule halves the disinflation.

(c) The rule asks for \(i = 2 + 0 + 1 \times (0 - 2) = 0\) percent with \(\bar{m} = 1\), exactly the floor, and for \(i = 2 + 0.5 + 2 \times (0.5 - 2) = -0.5\) percent with \(\bar{m} = 2\), which the central bank cannot set. With \(\bar{m} = 1\) the rule needs a negative rate one period later: \(2\pi_2 = 2 \times (-1.33) = -2.67\) percent.

Policy answer. On paper the board member is right. In practice, after a shock this large the aggressive rule needs a negative nominal rate from the very first period, and Problem 3 shows that the economy then spirals down instead of converging to \(C\). At the zero lower bound a stronger response has to come from other tools, such as asset purchases and forward guidance, or from fiscal policy.

Problem 10 (Challenge): Would faster price cuts have ended the Depression? A common intuition says that if wages and prices fell faster in a slump, the economy would recover sooner. Eggertsson (2010) showed that when the short-term nominal interest rate is zero and prices are falling, as in the Great Depression, a wish to work more, which pushes wages and prices down, can lower employment. Use the model of Figs. 12 and 13, with the Fed’s hike of 3 points and the crash \(\bar{a}' = -3\) held fixed. A larger slope \(\bar{\nu}\) of the Phillips curve means prices that react faster to a slump.

  1. Move \(\bar{\nu}\) from 0 to 0.75. How does output at \(D\) change?

  2. Derive output at \(D\) as a formula in \(\bar{a}'\), \(\bar{b}\), \(\bar{\nu}\) and the hike, and sign its derivative with respect to \(\bar{\nu}\). What does equation (11) add about the years after \(D\)?

  3. Now suppose the central bank follows the rule of Fig. 3 instead of freezing its nominal rate. Use equations (5) and

  1. to say whether a steeper Phillips curve helps or hurts after the 2008 shock. What is the policy lesson?
Hint

Follow depression_steps. At \(C\) output is \(\tilde{Y}_C = \bar{a}' - \bar{b} \times \text{hike}\); the slump lowers inflation by \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_C\), and with \(i\) fixed the real rate rises by as much (equation 8). For (c), look at where \(\bar{\nu}\) appears in the denominator \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\) of equations (5) and (7).

interact(great_depression,
         step=IntSlider(value=3, min=0, max=3, step=1, description="step (0 = A, 3 = D)", style=WIDE),
         hike=fixed(3.0), a_crash=fixed(-3.0),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.0, max=0.75, step=0.05, description="Phillips slope ν̄", style=WIDE),
         diagram=ToggleButtons(options=["IS/MP", "Phillips curve"], value="IS/MP", description="diagram"));

Source. The model of Figs. 12 and 13 above, adapted from Figs. 14.12 and 14.13 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) At step 3 the title shows output at \(D\) of −6.0 percent with \(\bar{\nu} = 0\), −7.5 with 0.25, −9.0 with 0.5 and −10.5 with 0.75. The faster prices react, the deeper the slump.

(b) Inflation starts at \(\pi_0 = 0\) and the nominal rate is \(i = \bar{r} + \text{hike}\). At \(C\), output is \(\tilde{Y}_C = \bar{a}' - \bar{b} \times \text{hike}\). The Phillips curve lowers inflation to \(\pi_D = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_C\), and with \(i\) fixed the Fisher equation (8) gives \(R_D = i - \pi_D = \bar{r} + \text{hike} - \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_C\). In the IS curve:

\[\tilde{Y}_D = \bar{a}' - \bar{b}\,(R_D - \bar{r}) = \bar{a}' - \bar{b} \times \text{hike} + \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_C = (1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu})\,(\bar{a}' - \bar{b} \times \text{hike}).\]

Its derivative is \(\partial\tilde{Y}_D/\partial\bar{\nu} = \bar{b}\,(\bar{a}' - \bar{b} \times \text{hike}) = 1 \times (-3 - 3) = -6 < 0\): each extra 0.25 of slope costs 1.5 points of output. Equation (11) adds that after \(D\) the gap keeps growing by the factor \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\) a year, which also rises with \(\bar{\nu}\): one year after \(D\) output would be \(1.5 \times (-9) = -13.5\) percent with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), and \(1.75 \times (-10.5) = -18.4\) percent with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.75\).

(c) With the rule, equation (5) gives first-year output \((\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f})/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\), and by equation (7) the share of the gap left each year is \(1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\). A larger \(\bar{\nu}\) makes both smaller:

for nu in [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]:
    point_D = depression_steps(nu=nu).loc[3]
    first = (A_HOUSING - B_BAR * F_CRISIS) / (1 + B_BAR * M_BAR * nu)     # equation (5), period 1
    share = 1 / (1 + B_BAR * M_BAR * nu)                                 # equation (7)
    print(f"nu = {nu:.2f}: frozen rate, Y~ at D = {point_D.Y:.1f}%;  "
          f"with the rule, first year Y~ = {first:.2f}%, gap left each year {share:.2f}")
nu = 0.00: frozen rate, Y~ at D = -6.0%;  with the rule, first year Y~ = -6.00%, gap left each year 1.00
nu = 0.25: frozen rate, Y~ at D = -7.5%;  with the rule, first year Y~ = -4.80%, gap left each year 0.80
nu = 0.50: frozen rate, Y~ at D = -9.0%;  with the rule, first year Y~ = -4.00%, gap left each year 0.67
nu = 0.75: frozen rate, Y~ at D = -10.5%;  with the rule, first year Y~ = -3.43%, gap left each year 0.57

With the rule, a steeper Phillips curve helps: the first-year recession is milder and the gap closes faster. The worst case is \(\bar{\nu} = 0\): inflation never falls, so the rule never cuts, and the gap of −6 percent never closes.

Policy lesson. Flexible prices stabilize the economy only when the central bank can turn falling inflation into a lower real interest rate. When the nominal rate is stuck, at zero or frozen as in the early 1930s, faster deflation raises the real rate and deepens the slump. In such a trap, pushing wages and prices down makes things worse; what helps is anything that raises reachable output in equation (10): higher expected inflation, a lower risk premium or a fiscal stimulus.
